label: Buckingham Palace
camera_source: Commons cluster (146 photos). Moved 87 m outwards on 2026-11-10 so it is 130 m from the subject's edge, as the text says.

text.description: Buckingham Palace is the official London residence and administrative headquarters of the monarch, and it is one of the easiest big buildings to photograph on the map. The long, pale stone front fits neatly into a phone frame, and the open space in front gives you room to step back. The palace grew from Buckingham House, a large townhouse built in 1703 for the Duke of Buckingham and Normanby. George III bought it in 1761, and in the early 19th century the architects John Nash and Edward Blore enlarged it around a central courtyard. The East Front, the part with the balcony where the royal family traditionally greets the crowds, was one of the last major additions. The palace has 775 rooms, and its garden is the largest private garden in London. From there you look south-west towards the building and can get the whole width in one shot, with the balcony, flagpole and any guards or crowds adding life to the frame. Expect other visitors in your picture, especially around ceremonial events. Take a few frames at different zoom levels, then check them on screen for tilted rooflines. Some of the palace's state rooms open to visitors in summer, so check the official site before you go if you want to go inside.
text.geographic_location: Buckingham Palace is in the City of Westminster, in central London.
text.directions_text: Start at Victoria Underground station (Circle line, District line and Victoria line) and head north. The palace is about 487 metres away, which is about 8 minutes on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the full front of the palace. If you are close and the building will not fit, switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x). Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as the balcony, the roofline or the flag.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on The Mall (looking west from the eastern end, toward the palace). A tree-lined view down the avenue with the Queen Victoria Memorial and the palace in the distance, including the flower beds.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the palace's horizontal edges with them so the building does not lean. Keep the phone level and at chest height, and leave some foreground, such as the open space, railings or people, to give a sense of scale. For a tighter shot, zoom to 2x or 3x and frame just the central balcony.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the palace front to set focus, then slide the exposure down a touch if the sky is bright, so the pale stone keeps its detail. Take a couple of shots in quick succession when people or flags are moving, and pick the sharpest.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early in the day is usually quieter, which gives you a cleaner view with fewer people in front of the palace. If you want a livelier picture, ceremonial events draw crowds, but you will have less room, so check the official site for dates.

text.access_note: The outside of the palace can be photographed from the surrounding public space. The state rooms are open to the public on selected dates, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Early in the day is usually quieter around the palace.

name: Big Ben and the Houses of Parliament
label: Big Ben
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/123557148: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Elizabeth Tower' (21 m across).

text.description: Big Ben is strictly the nickname of the Great Bell, but most people use it for the whole clock tower at the north end of the Palace of Westminster, which has been called the Elizabeth Tower since 2012. Pugin designed it in a Gothic Revival style, and it was completed in 1859. It stands about 96 metres tall, and each clock dial is almost 7 metres across, so the tower fills a phone frame easily and the golden-grey stonework and pointed spire make a strong, simple shape. The tower leans very slightly to the north-west, but you will not notice that in a photo. Look near the top for the Ayrton Light, a lantern above the belfry that is lit whenever the House of Commons sits after dark. The whole building is Grade I listed and part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Keep your phone upright and level so the tower does not appear to lean backwards. Pavements here can be busy, so take a few quick shots and then step aside. Check the clock face in your photo before moving on, as it is the detail most people want to see.
text.geographic_location: In Westminster, central London, at the north end of the Palace of Westminster, about 69 metres south-east of Westminster Underground station.
text.directions_text: Leave Westminster Underground station (Circle line, District line or Jubilee line) and the tower is about 1 minute on foot away, to the south-east. If you come by St. James's Park Underground station (Circle line and District line), the tower is about 12 minutes on foot to the east. The phone icon on the map is about 160 m south of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) from where you stand. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the tower and the long palace frontage together, or to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for a close shot of the clock face and spire.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 160 m south of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line a vertical grid line up with the tower's edge. Hold the phone upright and level, since tilting it back makes the tower look as if it is falling over. Leave a little sky above the spire and include some of the palace roofline below for scale.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the tower's stonework to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky stays blue and the clock face does not burn out. After dark, use night mode and rest your elbows against your body or a wall to keep the shot steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people. After dark, try night mode, and look for the Ayrton Light above the belfry, which is lit when the Commons is sitting.

text.access_note: The tower can be photographed from the public streets outside.
claims_not_in_sources: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people.
Pavements around the tower can be busy.

name: Tower of London
label: Tower of London
camera_source: Commons cluster (60 photos). Moved 61 m outwards on 2026-11-10 so it is 95 m from the subject's edge, as the text says.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/370870741: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Tower of London' (327 m across).

text.description:
The Tower of London is a medieval castle on the north bank of the Thames, and it makes a good subject because so many different shapes sit together: the pale White Tower in the middle, ringed by lower towers and walls. William the Conqueror built the White Tower in 1078, and it still rises about 27 metres at its southern battlements. The castle was later extended with two rings of defensive walls, and the whole site covers almost 12 acres. Over the centuries it has been a royal palace, a prison, an armoury, a treasury and the home of the Crown Jewels. Today it is a World Heritage Site, cared for by the charity Historic Royal Palaces.

That is far enough to fit a good part of the walls and towers into one frame, and near enough to pick out the stonework. The mix of old stone, battlements and the open space in front gives you layers to work with, which suits a phone camera well. Try one wide shot to show the scale, then a closer one of a single tower or section of wall. Keep your phone straight so the vertical walls don't lean, and take a few frames, as people often walk through the foreground.
text.geographic_location: The Tower of London stands on the north bank of the River Thames in the London Borough of Tower Hamlets. It sits just east of the City of London, beyond the open space of Tower Hill.
text.directions_text: Start at Tower Hill Underground station (Circle line and District line), which is about 3 minutes on foot from the Tower, with the castle to the south. Tower Gateway (DLR, the Docklands Light Railway) is about 5 minutes on foot away, with the Tower to the south-west. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole scene. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the walls and the sky in the frame. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the White Tower, battlements or a single turret from where you stand.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Trinity Square Gardens (south-facing part of the gardens at the top of Tower Hill). The Tower's stone turrets and medieval walls framed by greenery and lampposts in the foreground. From here you can see the walls and towers together without much of the foreground getting in the way.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the tops of the walls up with a horizontal line, so the towers don't lean. Leave a little space around the top of the highest tower rather than cropping tight. For a second shot, zoom in on one tower and let the stone texture fill the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stonework to set focus, then slide the exposure down a touch if the sky is bright and the walls look dark. Panorama mode can work for the long line of walls, but hold the phone steady and wait for passers-by to clear.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the stone and fewer people in the frame. Check the weather first, as an overcast day can flatten the stone but also gives even light with no harsh shadows.

text.access_note: The castle is cared for by Historic Royal Palaces, so check its official site for visiting details before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Early morning or late afternoon light is typically softer and crowds are usually smaller than midday.
Passers-by are likely to walk through the foreground in busy periods.

name: London Eye
label: London Eye
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/204068874: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'London Eye' (137 m across).

text.description:
The London Eye is a giant observation wheel on the South Bank of the River Thames, and it is easy to photograph because its shape is so simple. The rim is held by tensioned steel cables and looks like an enormous spoked bicycle wheel. Unusually, the whole thing is supported by an A-frame on one side only, so you can see a clear gap on the other. That one-sided design is worth showing in your picture.

The wheel is 135 metres tall, with a diameter of 120 metres. It was formally opened on 31 December 1999, but the public could not ride it until 9 March 2000. It stands between Westminster Bridge and Hungerford Bridge, beside County Hall. Its LED lighting was fitted in December 2006, so it can be lit in changing colours after dark.

Switch to the ultra-wide lens (0.5x), tilt the phone upwards and let the curve of the rim sweep across the picture. Keep the phone level, or the tall structure will look as if it is leaning. For a full view of the wheel, walk further back along the riverside. Use the telephoto lens (2x or more) to pick out the capsules and cables as close-up details.
text.geographic_location: On the South Bank of the River Thames in the London Borough of Lambeth, between Westminster Bridge and Hungerford Bridge. It sits beside County Hall, at the western end of Jubilee Gardens.
text.directions_text: Start from Waterloo Underground station (Bakerloo line, Jubilee line, Northern line and Waterloo & City line). The London Eye is about 413 metres to the west, about 7 minutes on foot. Head west towards the river and the wheel will soon be in sight. Westminster Underground station (Circle line, District line and Jubilee line) is another option, about 455 metres away, with the wheel to the north-east of the station. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide lens (0.5x), because you are very close to a very tall structure. Use the default lens (1x) for a tighter view of the lower part of the wheel and the A-frame. Use the telephoto lens (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for close-ups of the capsules and cables.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Step back along the riverside if you want the whole wheel in one frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the A-frame or the rim with a vertical line so the structure looks upright. With the ultra-wide lens, tilt the phone up and let the curve of the rim cross the frame. Try a second shot with the wheel's curve against the sky.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the wheel to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky keeps its colour and the wheel does not wash out. After dark, switch on night mode, rest your elbows on a wall or rail and hold still while it takes the shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Around dusk, the lit wheel stands out well against the darkening sky.

text.access_note: The riverside around the wheel is public space, but riding the wheel is a ticketed attraction, so check the official site before you go.

label: Borough Market

text.description: Borough Market is one of London's oldest and largest food markets, and it is a rewarding place for phone photos because so much happens in a small area. Stalls piled with fruit, cheese, bread and pastries sit under Victorian roofs and railway arches, with trains passing overhead. A market has stood on or near this site since at least the 12th century, although the present buildings date from the 1850s. The main design was by Henry Rose in 1851, and an Art Deco entrance was added on Southwark Street in 1932. One detail worth looking for is the South Portico, which came from the Floral Hall at Covent Garden and was re-erected here in 2004. It is now Grade II listed. The market also trades beneath the arches of the railway viaduct, which gives you strong lines, dark arches and bright stall displays in the same frame. It has appeared in films including Bridget Jones's Diary. For photos, start with a wide view to show the roofs and the busy walkways, then move in on colourful produce. Stalls are close together, so step to the side of the walkway before you stop to shoot, and ask a stallholder before taking a close photo of them. The retail market is closed on Mondays, so plan your visit for another day.
text.geographic_location: Borough Market is in Southwark, on the south bank of the Thames, just south of Southwark Cathedral and close to the southern end of London Bridge. It lies between Borough High Street and Southwark Street, and London Bridge Underground station is only a short walk away. The map marks the middle of the market's outline, which is about 221 m across.
text.directions_text: Start at London Bridge Underground station (Jubilee line and Northern line) and walk west to the market, about 2 minutes on foot. Alternatively, from Borough Underground station (Northern line), the market is to the north, about 9 minutes on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the roofs, arches and crowds. Then switch to the default lens (1x) for stalls and signs, and use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as pastries or cheeses from a polite distance.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (under the Victorian iron-and-glass roof, shooting up at the structure). The market's wrought-iron and glass roof framing the stalls, with light falling through in shafts. Keep to the edge of the walkway so you do not block people.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and use the lines of the roof and arches to lead the eye into the picture. Include a stall in the foreground to add colour and a sense of scale. For food close-ups, move closer or use the telephoto lens rather than leaning over the stall.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on a bright part of the scene to focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so the lit stalls do not wash out against the darker arches. Portrait mode suits single items of food. If a covered area is dim, try night mode and hold the phone steady against your body or a post.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Visit earlier in the day, when the walkways are usually quieter and you have more room to frame a shot. Come on any day except Monday, when the retail market is closed.

text.access_note: The market is a working retail market that is closed on Mondays, so check the official site before you go for current days and times.

label: Covent Garden

text.description: Covent Garden is the old fruit-and-vegetable market square on the eastern edge of the West End, now a lively mix of cafés, pubs, small shops and craft stalls. It photographs well because several things sit close together. There is a long, covered market building with a glass-and-iron feel, open space in front of it, and street performers who often draw a circle of onlookers. The church of St Paul's and the arcaded square were designed by Inigo Jones, commissioned in 1630. The square's layout was new to London at the time and went on to influence later estate planning. The market hall you see today dates from 1830, when Charles Fowler's neo-classical building was put up to cover the market. The wholesale market moved out in 1974, and the building reopened as a shopping centre in 1980. For a phone photo, aim for layers: the arches or roof in the background, people in the middle, and something close by, such as a café table or a performer's props, in the foreground. Keep an eye on the edges of the frame, because the square is busy and passers-by drift in and out. Take a few frames a second or two apart and pick the one where the gaps between people look best. If a performer is working the crowd, stay behind the audience, shoot over their heads rather than pushing in, and be ready to leave a tip if you stay for a while.
text.geographic_location: Covent Garden is in central London, on the eastern fringes of the West End, between St Martin's Lane and Drury Lane.
text.directions_text: The nearest station is Covent Garden Underground station (Piccadilly line), about 3 minutes on foot from the square, with the square to the south-east of the station. Leicester Square Underground station (Northern line and Piccadilly line) is also close, about 6 minutes on foot, with the square to the east of that station. The phone icon on the map is about 75 m north of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the whole market frontage and the roofline. Then switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural view of the crowd and performers. If your phone has a telephoto lens (2x-5x), use it for details such as signs, flower baskets or a performer's expression.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 75 m north of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south. If the ground is crowded, step a little to one side so people pass behind you, not through the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the building's vertical columns with the grid so the shot looks straight. Leave some open space in the lower third for people walking, and use the arches as a natural frame if you move closer. Hold the phone level to stop the buildings leaning inwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the building to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the bright sky or glass roof washes out the picture. A Live Photo can capture a performer's movement, and in the evening night mode helps if you hold the phone steady against a pillar or rail.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning usually means fewer people and a clearer view of the architecture. Later in the day the square is livelier and the performers are out, which suits people-focused shots. In the evening the lit-up arcades suit night mode.

text.access_note: The square is a public area with shops, cafés and performers around it, but individual venues and market stalls may have their own rules and hours, so check the official site before you go.

name: Tower Bridge
label: Tower Bridge
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/2079674503: the OpenStreetMap point 'Tower Bridge'.

text.description: Tower Bridge is the one that looks like a Victorian castle crossing the Thames: two stone-clad towers, blue-painted suspension sections and a pair of high walkways joining the towers at the top. That strong, symmetrical shape is why it photographs so easily, because even a quick snap gives you a clear subject. The bridge was built between 1886 and 1894 and opened on 30 June 1894. The architect Horace Jones and the engineer John Wolfe Barry designed it, and the law required it to fit in with the nearby Tower of London. It is about 290 m long and each tower is 65 m tall. The middle section is made of two bascules, or leaves, that lift to let ships through. Try one wide shot of the whole structure, then a closer one of a single tower and the walkway above the road. The road across the bridge is open to everyone on foot, so you can also take photos while crossing. People often mix this bridge up with London Bridge, which is further upstream, so check that Tower Bridge is your subject if you are unsure.
text.geographic_location: Tower Bridge crosses the River Thames in central London, right beside the Tower of London. It links the north and south banks of the river.
text.directions_text: The nearest station is Tower Hill Underground station (Circle line and District line). From there the bridge is to the south, about 8 minutes on foot. Tower Gateway station (DLR, the Docklands Light Railway) is also nearby, with the bridge to the south of the station, about 9 minutes on foot. The phone icon on the map is about 90 m south-west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit both towers, the walkways and some sky. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural look, or use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out a single tower or the walkway.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 90 m south-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-east.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and line up the two towers so they are level and upright. Keep the phone straight and not tilted upwards, so the towers don't lean inwards. Try one wide shot with the full bridge and a foreground of water or railings. Then take a tighter shot of one tower and the blue suspension sections.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the bridge to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky stays blue and the stonework keeps its detail. After dark, use night mode and brace your elbows on a railing or wall. Hold still until the capture finishes. For a panorama, hold the phone upright and sweep slowly. Moving traffic and people may blur or smear.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning and late afternoon usually give softer light and fewer people. Just after sunset, the bridge looks good against a darkening sky once its lights are on.

text.access_note: The bridge deck is open to pedestrians and vehicles, but the towers, high-level walkways and engine rooms are part of the Tower Bridge Exhibition, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: From the stand-here point, south-west of the bridge and facing north-east, the sun is behind you in the late afternoon and evening, so it lights the bridge face-on.

text.description:
The Shard is a slim glass pyramid that rises above Southwark and, at 309.6 metres and 95 storeys, is the tallest building in the United Kingdom. Architect Renzo Piano designed it as a spire, drawing on church steeples in old views of London, ships' masts and the railway lines beside the site. Construction began in 2009, and it was inaugurated on 5 July 2012. The public viewing gallery, The View from The Shard, opened on 1 February 2013.

The tower photographs well because of its glass skin. About 11,000 angled panes were designed to catch the sunlight and sky, so the building looks different with the weather and the seasons. On a clear day it can look pale and sharp. On a grey day it blends softly into the clouds.

The phone icon on the map is at the Shard itself, so you are right at the foot of the tower, looking almost straight up. That suits dramatic, converging lines, but your phone will not fit the whole building into one shot from here. For a full-height picture, walk back along the nearby streets until the whole spire fits in the frame. Keep your phone upright and use the gridlines to stop the sides leaning. Wipe your lens first, as glass and sky can show every smudge. Watch for people and traffic at the edges of the frame, especially around the busy station.
text.geographic_location: The Shard stands in Southwark, in central London, on the south side of the River Thames, close to London Bridge Underground station.
text.directions_text: Start at London Bridge Underground station (Jubilee line and Northern line). The Shard is about 3 minutes on foot from the station, to the south-east. Alternatively, Borough Underground station (Northern line) is about 10 minutes on foot away, with the Shard to the north-east. Once you can see the tower, head towards it and stop at the phone icon on the map. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) at the phone icon on the map, because you are very close to the tower. Switch to the default lens (1x) as you walk back for a more natural shape. If your phone has telephoto (2x-5x), use it from a distance to pick out the glass facets and the pointed top.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. The building rises straight above you. Take your close-up looking-up shots here.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up one edge of the tower with a vertical line to keep it straight. When looking up, tilt the phone as little as you can, because the more you tilt it, the more the sides lean inwards. Use a nearby lamp post, a bus or people at the bottom of the frame to give a sense of scale.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the tower to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the bright sky does not wash out the glass. After dark, use night mode and brace your elbows against your body to keep the shot steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: A clear day with blue sky gives the glass a bright, sharp look. Late afternoon and dusk often add warm reflections and lit windows, and at dusk night mode works well.

text.access_note: The tower's base is surrounded by public streets, but the building itself is private, so check the official site before you go if you want to visit the viewing gallery.

text.description:
The Great Court is a central space within the British Museum in Bloomsbury. It is a bright, open courtyard under a glass roof, so it is easy to photograph even on a grey London day. The roof's pattern of lines and the pale stonework give you plenty of shapes to work with, and the crowds add a sense of scale.

The museum itself has a long story. It was established in 1753 as the world's first public national museum, and it opened its doors in 1759 in Montagu House, on the same site as today's building. Admission is free apart from loan exhibitions, and it drew more than six million visitors in 2025, so expect company.

For a phone, this is a place for wide, airy pictures. Stand in the open middle of the court and use the ultra-wide (0.5x) to catch the roof and the curve of the walls. Switch to the default lens (1x) for pictures of people walking through, and try the telephoto for the roof's pattern or small architectural details. Keep your phone level, with gridlines switched on, because straight lines look wrong when tilted. Wipe the lens first, and be ready to wait a moment for a gap in the crowd.
text.geographic_location: The Great Court is at the heart of the British Museum in Bloomsbury, central London, a short walk from Russell Square Underground station and Tottenham Court Road Underground station.

text.description:
The Victoria and Albert Museum, usually called the V&A, is the world's largest museum of applied arts, decorative arts and design, with a collection of more than 2.8 million objects. The South Kensington site covers 12.5 acres and has over 145 galleries. That is far too much to cover in one visit, so a few well-chosen pictures work better than trying to photograph everything.

The story behind the place adds interest to your photos. The museum grew out of the Government School of Design, set up in 1832, and moved to this part of London in 1857. Queen Victoria officially opened it on 20 June 1857. Henry Cole even persuaded the authorities to rename the area South Kensington, because the old name, Brompton, was thought unattractive.

Stand back, keep the building square to you, and use the gridlines to keep the vertical lines straight. Then step closer for details such as doorways, stonework and people passing through the entrance. Inside, galleries are often dimly lit, so hold the phone steady against your body or a wall.

Entrance to the museum is free. Even so, check the official site before you go for current access and any special exhibitions.

If you are coming from Gloucester Road station (also Circle, District and Piccadilly lines on the Underground), the museum is to the east, about 14 minutes on foot (about 853 m). shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (in front of the main entrance facade, Cromwell Road frontage). The terracotta main facade with the central tower and crown spire, framed straight-on from the pavement across Cromwell Road.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and line up the building's vertical edges with them so the walls do not lean. Leave a little space at the bottom for people walking past, which gives a sense of scale. Then take a closer, tighter shot of one detail.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the building to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the stonework does not wash out. In dim galleries, let night mode work and keep the phone still until it finishes.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light is usually kinder to the building than harsh midday sun. Arriving early also tends to mean fewer people in your shots.

name: Trafalgar Square

text.description: Trafalgar Square is one of central London's great open spaces, and it photographs well because so much is packed into one view. Nelson's Column stands in the middle, 169 feet (52 m) tall, with the fountains and four bronze lions around its base. The columns and pale stone of the National Gallery run along the north side, and the church of St Martin-in-the-Fields sits to the east. The square opened in 1844 and is named after the Battle of Trafalgar of 1805. It also stands on the old Charing Cross, the point from which distances from London are measured. Look for the fourth plinth, which has held a changing series of artworks since 1999, so there is often something unexpected to put in the frame. At Christmas the square gets a tree donated by Norway, and New Year's Eve is a big occasion here. For a phone photo, aim for a clear, simple view of the column with the lions or fountain in front of it, then take a second wider shot that shows the buildings around the square. Keep the column upright by using the gridlines, and try portrait orientation to fit its full height.
text.geographic_location: Trafalgar Square is in the City of Westminster in Central London, at Charing Cross, directly in front of the National Gallery. Nelson's Column, the subject of this shot, stands in the middle of the square at about 51.5078° N, 0.1279° W. The Mall, Whitehall and the Strand all lead off from it.
text.directions_text: Start at Charing Cross Underground station (Bakerloo line and Northern line), the nearest station. Nelson's Column is 80 m to the south-west of it, about 1 minute on foot. shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the column with the lions and fountain, then switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the open square and the surrounding buildings. The telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) is good for the statue at the top of the column and for details of the lions.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 110 m north-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-east. Nelson's Column stands in the centre of the square.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn the phone upright and put the column on the centre gridline, with the lions or the fountain at the bottom of the frame. For a second shot, turn the phone sideways at 0.5x and let the open square fill the picture. Keep the phone level so the column does not lean.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the sky near the top of the column to set focus and brightness, then use the exposure slider to lower the brightness slightly if the sky is washing out. After dark, night mode can help; hold the phone as still as you can and rest your elbows against your body.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early in the morning is usually quieter, which makes it easier to get a clear view of the column. Evening gives you the option of night shots, and the Christmas tree is in place for twelve days before and after Christmas Day.

text.description: Piccadilly Circus is a busy road junction and public space in London's West End, built in 1819 to link Regent Street with Piccadilly. A "circus" here simply means a round open space where streets meet, although the junction lost its circular shape in the 1880s. Today it is a meeting place in its own right, with theatres, shops and restaurants all around. It photographs well because so much happens in one view: the big video screens and signs on the corner building to the north, red buses crossing the junction, and the Shaftesbury Memorial Fountain on the south-western corner. The fountain was put up in 1893, and its winged statue is of Anteros, though many people believe it is Eros. The screens now use LED displays, which replaced the old neon signs by 2011, so the colours change constantly and every shot looks a little different. Keep your phone strap or grip secure and be ready for people walking into your shot, because the crowds rarely thin out. Take a few frames in a row and pick the one with the cleanest foreground. Stay well back from the kerb when buses and taxis pass.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the whole junction, the screens and the fountain together. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural view. shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 50 m north-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-east. Keep clear of the kerb and the crowds passing through.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the horizon of the building rooflines on the upper third line. Let a bus or a few pedestrians fill the foreground to add scale. For a tighter shot, use the fountain as a small foreground element and the lit screens as the backdrop. Keep your phone upright so the vertical lines of the buildings stay straight.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brightest screen to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the colours do not wash out. After dark, use night mode and hold the phone steady against your body for the exposure time. Live Photos can catch moving buses as light trails.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Dusk and after dark, when the screens are at their most vivid and the sky behind them is still deep blue.

text.description: Tate Modern is the national gallery of international modern and contemporary art, and it sits inside the former Bankside Power Station on the south bank of the Thames. That is why it photographs so well: the building is a huge, plain brick block with a tall central chimney, and it looks more like a cathedral of industry than a gallery. Sir Giles Gilbert Scott designed the power station, and it was built in two stages between 1947 and 1963. It was about 200 m long, and the chimney stands 99 m high. The power station closed in 1981, and the gallery opened in the converted building on 11 May 2000. A ten-storey tower, 65 m high, was added on the south side and opened in 2016. It has a sloping brick-latticework face that echoes the old brickwork, so you can get old and new in one picture. The building is directly across the river from St Paul's Cathedral. Step back as far as the space allows and shoot upwards to include the chimney. Look for strong vertical and horizontal lines, such as brick edges and the glass roof extension, and use them to keep your picture tidy. People walking past give a useful sense of scale. Inside is a separate matter, as the rules for photography and tickets can change, so check the official site before you go.

text.description:
Harrods is the big department store on Brompton Road in Knightsbridge, and its sheer scale is what makes it so photogenic. The building was designed by C. W. Stephens for Charles Digby Harrod and opened in 1905. It stands on the site where his father, Charles Henry Harrod, took over a small shop in 1849, and an earlier store there was destroyed by fire. Today it is described as the largest department store in Europe, with around 1.1 million square feet of selling space, and its building has been Grade II* listed since 1969. About 15 million people were said to visit each year as of 2023, so expect people in the foreground of most shots.

From there you can take in a good stretch of the long frontage, with the repeating windows and ornate stonework giving the picture a strong rhythm. Keep your phone level so the vertical lines stay straight. Include a little street life, such as a passing bus or people on the pavement, to give a sense of scale and of the busy Knightsbridge setting. Then step closer for a second, tighter shot of one section of the façade, a doorway or a window display.

The store is a working shop, so only photograph from public pavements unless you have checked the rules for going inside.

text.description:
Camden Market is a group of neighbouring markets in Camden Town, set in and around the old Pickfords stables and beside the Regent's Canal. That mix of working-canal history and bustling stalls is what makes it so good to photograph. Brick and cast-iron buildings, railway arches, footbridges and ramps sit alongside colourful shopfronts, street food counters and hand-painted signs, so there is something to point a phone at in almost every direction.

A few facts help you read what you see. The weekly crafts market near Camden Lock began on 30 March 1974 and grew into the large complex of today. The three-storey market hall on the original Lock site opened in 1991, built in brick and cast iron to echo the area's 19th-century industrial buildings. Part of the Stables Market is in the former Pickfords horse hospital, which is Grade II listed, and many units are set into railway arches.

For photos, look for layers: stall fronts in the foreground, old brickwork and ironwork behind, and people walking through the middle. Take a wide view first to show the setting, then move closer for details such as signs, food stalls and shopfront colours. The weekend is the busiest trading period, so expect crowds in your frame at those times. Keep your phone in a secure hand or on a wrist strap near the canal edge.
text.geographic_location: Camden Market is in Camden Town, north London, just north of the Hampstead Road Lock on the Regent's Canal, often called Camden Lock. It sits in and around the old Pickfords stables, close to Chalk Farm Road, and lies north-west of Camden Town Underground station and south-east of Chalk Farm Underground station.

Include some old brick or ironwork to show the history, and keep the horizon level. For a detail shot, fill the frame with one colourful sign or food counter.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brightest part of a busy scene to focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so signs and lights do not wash out. In the evening, use night mode and hold the phone against a wall or rail to keep it steady. Try a Live Photo in the crowds to choose the best moment afterwards.

text.description: Portobello Road is the long, gently winding street at the heart of Notting Hill, and it is a good place for lively street photographs on a phone. Terraced houses and shopfronts crowd together along curving lanes, and on market days stalls fill the road with colour, signs and people. The market section is about 940 metres long. Saturday is the main day, when all five sections open: second-hand goods, clothing and fashion, household essentials, food, and antiques. It is described as the largest antiques market in the UK. The street began as a country lane called Green's Lane and became built-up in the second half of the 19th century. That is why the Victorian terraces and shops sit so tightly together. Many visitors also know it from the 1999 film Notting Hill, which was filmed largely on the street. For photographs, look for a view along the road with stalls on both sides, then move in for close shots of fruit, antiques and shop signs. Take a few wide frames first, then pick out details. Keep your phone in a pocket or wrist strap while you walk through crowds, and step to the edge of the pavement before you stop to shoot so you do not block people.

text.description:
The Sky Garden sits at the top of 20 Fenchurch Street, the 160 m, 38-storey tower that London nicknamed "the Walkie-Talkie" because its top-heavy shape looks a little like a handset. Architect Rafael Viñoly designed it, and it was finished in spring 2014. The garden itself, a viewing deck with a terrace, bar and restaurants across the top three floors, opened in January 2015. It is reached by two express lifts.

There are two kinds of photo here. From outside, the tower's bulging, outward-leaning top makes a strong shape against the sky, and the dense streets of the City of London give you plenty of layers to work with. From inside, the viewing area gives you a high look out over the city, which suits wide scenes with lots of rooftops.

The tower is also known for a sunlight quirk. During construction it was found that, on sunny days, the curved glass could focus light onto the streets to the south for a short time each day. A permanent awning was added in 2014. So if the sun is out, expect strong glare and reflections on the building's glass.

For the best results, keep your phone lens clean, hold the phone steady with both hands and check your edges for leaning verticals. Entry to the garden has restrictions, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: In the historic City of London financial district, on Fenchurch Street, just east of Monument Underground station and Bank station.
text.directions_text: The nearest station is Monument Underground station (Circle line and District line), about 3 minutes on foot, with the tower to the east of the station. Bank station (Central line, Northern line, Waterloo & City line and the DLR, the Docklands Light Railway) is also close, at about 7 minutes on foot, and the tower lies to the east of it too. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Outside, use the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the tall, top-heavy tower in from close range. Use the default lens (1x) for a calmer, less stretched view. If your phone has telephoto/zoom (2x-5x), use it to pick out the top of the tower or details of the glass.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From there, point the phone upwards to show the building's shape. If you want the whole tower in the frame, walk a little way down the street and turn back to face it. Inside the garden, you stand at the windows or terrace and shoot outwards instead.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the edges of the tower with the vertical lines to keep it from looking as if it leans. Include a slice of sky above the wider top and some nearby buildings to show scale. Inside, keep a railing or window edge out of the corners and look for rooftops layered one behind another.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brightest part of the sky or the building, then pull the exposure slider down slightly to keep the glass from burning out. Inside, press the lens close to the window, or shade it with your hand, to reduce reflections. Night mode can help on dim days or in the evening.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a clear day so there is some sky and definition in the glass. Late afternoon or around sunset usually gives softer, warmer light. Remember that bright sun can cause strong glare on the glass.

text.access_note: The garden is on the top floors of an office tower and is open to the public only with restrictions, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Views from the viewing area are across the City and its surrounding rooftops.
Late afternoon or sunset light is usually softer and warmer than midday light.
Pressing a phone lens close to glass or shading it with a hand reduces reflections.
The ultra-wide lens helps fit a tall building into the frame from close range.
Gridlines help keep vertical lines upright when pointing a phone upwards.

name: Battersea Power Station
label: Battersea Power Stn
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/4965216: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Battersea Power Station' (257 m across).
notes: Now a shopping and leisure site: many searches are shopping.

text.description:
Battersea Power Station is the four-chimney brick landmark on the south bank of the Thames in Nine Elms. It was built in two halves: the western half between 1929 and 1935, and a near-identical eastern half that came into operation between 1953 and 1955. The second half mirrors the first, which is why the building looks so symmetrical. Giles Gilbert Scott was brought in to design the exterior, and the building is counted among the world's largest brick buildings. It was decommissioned between 1975 and 1983, stood largely unused for decades, and the main building opened to the public in October 2022 as part of a redevelopment of a 42-acre (17 ha) site. It is Grade II* listed, and it also appeared on the cover of Pink Floyd's 1977 album Animals.

It photographs well because the shape is so simple and strong: a huge brick block with a chimney at each corner. The straight lines and repeated windows suit gridlines, and a clear sky behind the chimneys keeps the picture clean. Take a few frames at different zoom levels: one wide shot for the whole building, and a tighter one for brickwork and chimney tops. Wipe your lens before you start, as a smeared lens softens the detail in the brick.
text.geographic_location: Battersea Power Station stands on the south bank of the River Thames in Nine Elms, in the London Borough of Wandsworth, in south-west London.
text.directions_text: Take the Northern line (Underground) to Battersea Power Station Underground station. The power station building lies to the north of the station, about 269 m away, which is about 4 minutes on foot. The phone icon on the map is about 85 m north-east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x), because the building is large and you are standing close to it. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural look with less edge stretching. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for chimney tops and brick texture.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 85 m north-east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-west.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up a chimney or wall edge with a vertical grid line so the building does not lean. Hold the phone level, as tilting upwards makes the walls slope inwards. Try one frame with all four chimneys and one tighter shot with just the brick wall and two chimneys.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brickwork to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky looks washed out. Keep the 0.5x lens for wide shots and check the corners for stretching.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer, warmer light on the brick. A day with some cloud texture in the sky makes the chimneys stand out. After dark, try night mode and hold the phone steady against something solid.

text.access_note: The main building opened to the public in October 2022 and parts of it may be ticketed or restricted, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Early morning or late afternoon light is usually softer and warmer on brick.
You can view and photograph the building from the area around the stand-here point without going inside.
Tilting a phone upwards makes tall walls appear to lean inwards (perspective distortion).
Ultra-wide lenses can stretch objects near the edges of the frame.

name: Natural History Museum Hintze Hall
label: Natural History Museum
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/24436446: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Natural History Museum' (313 m across).
notes: Only 'natural history museum london' would be safe: the bare name also means other cities' museums. Both are counted here; doubtful.

text.description:
The central hall of the Natural History Museum is the room most visitors remember, and it works well for phone photos. The Victorian building was designed by Alfred Waterhouse in his own Romanesque style, and the interior and exterior make extensive use of architectural terracotta tiles. Look up and you will see the vaulted space, repeating arches and carved detail. A blue whale skeleton hangs from the ceiling, in the place where a Diplodocus cast stood until 2017. The museum is sometimes called a cathedral of nature, and standing under the whale you can see why.

The building opened on 18 April 1881 after construction began in 1873. It now holds some 80 million specimens, and the sources note that it does not charge an admission fee.

For photos, the main challenge is scale. The hall is tall and the whale is long, so step back as far as is comfortable and tilt the phone slightly upwards. Keep the phone level from side to side so the arches don't lean. Include a person in the frame, such as a friend or a stranger in the distance, to show how big the whale is. Then move in for close shots of the terracotta and the carved detail. Expect other visitors in most frames, so be patient and shoot between groups.
text.geographic_location: The Natural History Museum is in South Kensington, London, on Exhibition Road and Cromwell Road, close to the Science Museum and the Victoria and Albert Museum. The main frontage is on Cromwell Road. South Kensington Underground station is the nearest station, about 330 m away.
text.directions_text: Start at South Kensington Underground station, served by the Circle line, District line and Piccadilly line. The museum is about 328 m to the north-west, about 5 minutes on foot. Alternatively, Gloucester Road Underground station (Circle line, District line and Piccadilly line) is about 570 m to the west of the museum, which is about 9 minutes on foot heading east. The main frontage is on Cromwell Road. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole whale and the arches into one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural look, then use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details like the terracotta and carvings.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Stand inside the central hall, as far back from the whale as you can comfortably get, and angle the phone upwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the arches up with the vertical lines so the walls stay straight. Centre the whale for a symmetrical shot, or place it off to one side and let the arches lead the eye. Try one shot with a person in the frame for scale.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the whale to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so bright areas don't wash out. If your phone switches to night mode indoors, hold it still with your elbows against your body for a sharper shot. Panorama works poorly in a busy hall, so take a few separate shots instead.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Visit soon after opening or later in the day, when the hall is usually quieter. Check the museum's website for current opening times.

text.access_note: The sources say entry to the museum is free, but check the official site before you go for opening times and any booking or entry rules.
claims_not_in_sources: The museum's central hall is called Hintze Hall (taken from the spot name).
The hall is usually quieter soon after opening or later in the day than in the middle of the day.
Phone cameras may switch to night mode in indoor lighting.
Panorama mode struggles with moving crowds.

name: St Paul's Cathedral
label: St Paul's
camera_source: Commons cluster (101 photos). Moved 58 m outwards on 2026-11-10 so it is 100 m from the subject's edge, as the text says.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/369161987: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'St Paul's Cathedral' (179 m across).
notes: Photography inside is not allowed (to be checked); the spot is the outside and the view from the Millennium Bridge.

text.description:
St Paul's Cathedral is the big domed church on Ludgate Hill, the highest point of the City of London. Sir Christopher Wren designed it in the English Baroque style, and it was completed in 1710 as part of the rebuilding after the Great Fire of London. The cathedral is 111 m (365 ft) high, topped by its dome. It was the tallest building in London from 1710 to 1963 and is still counted among the highest domes in the world. That height and the pale stonework make it easy to recognise, and it is a gift for a phone camera because the shape reads clearly even in a small frame.

The distance gives you room to fit a lot of the building in one shot, with the dome rising behind the front. The main challenge is size: up close, the building is too tall for a single frame unless you use a wide lens and tilt the phone upwards. Stepping back is usually better than leaning back. Keep the phone upright and level, and use the gridlines to stop the columns leaning inwards. People will walk through your picture, so take a few frames and pick the one with the cleanest foreground.

The cathedral is a working church with daily services, so be quiet and respectful near the doors. Photography inside may be restricted, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: St Paul's Cathedral stands on Ludgate Hill in the City of London, at the highest point of the old city, with the middle of its outline at about 51.51377° N, 0.09848° W.
text.directions_text: Start at St. Paul's Underground station on the Central line; the cathedral is about 3 minutes on foot, to the south of the station. From Mansion House Underground station (Circle and District lines) it is about 5 minutes on foot, heading north-west. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) from where you stand. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you move closer and the top of the dome will not fit. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as the dome or the carved stonework.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Millennium Bridge (Southbank end, standing just left of the bridge in front of Tate Modern, looking north). The cathedral's dome sits at the far end of the bridge's straight line, with the Thames and the bridge's steel lines framing it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the columns and towers with the vertical lines so the building does not lean. Keep the dome in the upper part of the frame and leave some open ground at the bottom for scale. Try one wide shot and one closer shot with the telephoto.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the pale stonework to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the stone keeps its detail against a bright sky. Panorama mode is worth trying if you stay at this distance, but hold the phone upright and turn slowly.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning usually has fewer people. In the afternoon or at golden hour the west front may catch warmer light. In dim light, use night mode and brace your elbows against your body to keep the phone steady.

text.access_note: The cathedral is a working church with a tourist entry fee at the door, so check the official site before you go for current access and photography rules.
claims_not_in_sources: The side of the cathedral seen from the stand-here point (to its west) is the main front with the twin towers.
Early mornings are usually quieter around the cathedral.
The west front may catch warmer light in the afternoon or at golden hour.
Photography inside the cathedral may be restricted.
The building is too tall to fit in one frame at close range without a wide lens.
